Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Utilities Inc. Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode until we open the call up for questions following today's presentation. During the Q&A session, please press star then one if using a touch-tone phone to ask a question. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Jennifer Brooks, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Jennifer Brooks: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Utilities's Q2 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me today from management are Lisa Chen, our Chief Executive Officer; Mike Harlan, our Chief Financial Officer; Alex Rivera, our Chief Operating Officer; Karen Voss, our Chief Strategy Officer; and Brian Walsh, our Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that statements made during this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our SEC filings for a detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Jennifer, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on our performance this quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities, delivering solid results in a challenging environment.

Our performance was driven by:
1. Retirement of fossil fuel plants and replacement strategies.
2. Progress towards clean energy goals and emission reductions.
3. Rate base growth and factors impacting growth.
4. Dividend policy and payout ratio strategy.
5. Successful integration of Desert Bloom solar farm.
6. Advancement of our Net-Zero by 2045 program.

Let me provide some more detail on these six key aspects.

Starting with our retirement of fossil fuel plants and replacement strategies. As we wrap up our Q2 results, one of our most transformative strategic pillars has been the accelerated retirement of our legacy fossil fuel fleet and our comprehensive replacement approaches. This goes beyond mere compliance—it's about positioning Apex Utilities, a leading integrated utility and independent power producer in the Midwest and Southeast, to deliver superior risk-adjusted returns in a decarbonizing grid while addressing surging demand from electrification, electric vehicles, and hyperscale data centers.

The numbers tell the story. Over the past 24 months, we've successfully retired 1,200 MW of coal-fired capacity across three plants in the MISO South footprint—our Big River and Prairie Wind units, which originated in the 1970s. These retirements reduced our annual O&M expenses by $180 million, mainly from fuel costs and emissions compliance under the EPA's updated Mercury and Air Toxics Standards. Ahead, we're set to retire another 1,800 MW by the end of 2026, including our final 800 MW subcritical coal block at Heartland Station. Overall, fleet decommissioning now accounts for 45% of our 8 GW thermal portfolio, in line with our 2030 net-zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions goal.

The timing makes economic sense. Unhedged coal plants are operating below 30% utilization in MISO capacity auctions, where clearing prices for renewables and storage have dropped to $20-40 per kW-year. After the IRA, the levelized cost of energy for new solar-plus-storage hybrids is $28-35 per MWh, compared to $45-55 per MWh to retrofit coal with carbon capture and storage. We've secured 85% of retirements through FERC-approved settlements with state commissions, avoiding stranded asset risks and gaining $450 million in regulatory recovery via multi-year rate cases in Illinois and Missouri.

On replacements, we're oversizing to support growth. In Q2, we energized 650 MW of replacement capacity, led by the 400 MW Desert Bloom solar farm in ERCOT, paired with 200 MWh of Tesla Megapack storage. This $550 million project, 60% debt-financed at our 4.2% blended cost of capital, qualifies for the full 40% ITC under the IRA's domestic content and energy communities adders. Initial performance beats pro forma: 32% DC capacity factor against 26% modeled, due to bifacial Trina Vertex modules and Nextracker single-axis tracking.

Our pipeline is strong at 3.2 GW under construction or late-stage development, including 1.2 GW onshore wind in SPP with Vestas V150-4.2 MW turbines under 15-year PPAs at $25 per MWh all-in, hedged against PTC phaseout; 800 MW standalone battery storage in PJM with Fluence Gridstack for 4-hour duration, projecting $15 million yearly from ancillary services; and 400 MW combined-cycle gas in the Southeast with GE Vernova 7HA units hydrogen-ready for up to 30% blending now, scaling to 100% by 2035 per DOE goals. We've also approved two hybrid nuclear uprates adding 150 MW at our Browns Ferry-adjacent site through an SMR partnership with NuScale, accessing DOE's $2.5 billion advanced reactor funding.

Regionally, it varies. In MISO, with 5 GW coal retirements announced YTD like Ameren's 4.2 GW plan, we're focusing on dispatchable hybrids to counter 8-12% renewables curtailment during duck curve peaks. ERCOT's 15% YoY load growth from Bitcoin mining and AI favors our solar-storage, clearing the latest CREZ auction 25% below gas peakers. In California, we're eyeing CAISO imports via 500 kV upgrades, but RPS mandates highlight our Midwest strengths.

This optimizes our portfolio. Our approved IRP in four states models 12% ROE on $4.2 billion capex through 2028, with 70% IRA incentives to equity. We've derisked with 15-year corporate PPAs with Google and Microsoft covering 40% new capacity at $30-35 per MWh. Partnerships include co-development with NextEra on 1 GW offshore wind in Lake Michigan and a $200 million DOE grant for Form Energy's long-duration iron-air batteries.

Risks include 2 TW national interconnection queues, but our 95% success rate from colocation on retired sites cuts 18 months off timelines. Supply chain is mixed—U.S. polysilicon via First Solar Series 7, 80% turbine hedges through 2026.

Overall, these deliver $250 million annual FCF by 2027, with 8% rate base CAGR. We're leading the shift, akin to Duke's coal-to-renewables pivot boosting TSR 150% over five years.

Next, our continued growth in the renewable energy portfolio and progress towards clean energy goals and emission reductions. Good morning again—before moving on, a detailed update on our clean energy momentum, core to our strategy at Apex Utilities. We're targeting net-zero Scope 1 and 2 by 2045, with 80% reduction from 2019 baseline by 2035, aligned with Science Based Targets and U.S. Paris commitments.

Year-to-date, system-wide CO2 emissions dropped 28% YoY to 42 million metric tons, ahead of trajectory via fleet optimization and clean additions. Intensity at 320 grams CO2/kWh, down 12% from last Q2 and 18% below EIA utility average, on pace for 35% portfolio reduction by 2024 end.

Renewables now 45% of our 28,000 MW capacity, up from 38% end-2023, with 1.2 GW added YTD. Q2 saw 450 MW utility-scale solar in ERCOT and MISO South, under PPAs with Google and Microsoft for 85% output at $28/MWh blended over 15 years. Capacity factors at 28% with First Solar bifacials and trackers.

Wind added 350 MW in Plains, including 200 MW Oklahoma with 100 MW/200 MWh Fluence BESS at 45% effective CF, earning $15 million in ERCOT frequency regulation YTD. Ahead, 800 MW offshore wind Northeast with Ørsted JV, Phase 1 permitted, construction Q2 2025 at $40/MWh LCOE via IRA PTC.

On thermal decarbonization, CCUS at 1,200 MW Heritage Coal captures 1.2 million tons CO2 yearly at 92% efficiency with ExxonMobil tech, extending life and yielding $45 million from 45Q credits. Green H2 blending at two PJM gas peakers up to 20% from 10 MW electrolyzer, no derates, for 2026 scale.

Regionally positive: Southeast solar at 30% mix per Georgia IRP/RPS; Southwest 15% cuts from 400 MW gas retirement offset by 600 MW solar-storage; Midwest coal belt accelerated by EPA rules, hedged with 500,000 RECs at $5.50/MWh.

Leveraging IRA: $1.2 billion ITC/PTC YTD, Qcells domestic bonuses. MOU with TerraPower for two 345 MW SMRs by 2030 at <$60/MWh LCOE. Supply delays like Vestas blades offset by DOE $7B hydrogen hubs.

Financially accretive: clean ROIC 9.5% vs. thermal 7%, 15% to EPS growth. Raising 2025 renewable capex to $2.8 billion, 60% green bonds at 4.2%.

This builds a moat for EV/data center demand.

Moving to rate base growth and factors impacting it, which ties to our infrastructure investments. Our rate base is the foundation of our regulated returns. As of June 30, consolidated rate base at $28.7 billion, up 6.2% YoY from $27.0 billion, with $1.8 billion trailing 12-month organic growth and $450 million quarter-over-quarter. On track for 5.5-6.5% full-year growth to ~$29.5 billion, at upper end of 5-6% five-year CAGR, beating EEI 4.5% average and peers like Duke/Southern.

Midwest (MISO) led at 7.1% YoY, West (CAISO/WECC) 5.3%. Beats Xcel 5.8%, PG&E 4-5%.

Driven by $2.8 billion 2024 capex, 85% regulated: 45% transmission/grid mod ($1.25B)—e.g., $650M Ironwood-Horizon 345 kV 120-mile line 75% complete, adding $500M CWIP; AMI 2.0 for 1.2M endpoints, $120M via DERMS for data centers (15-20 GW by 2030 per MISO LDA).

30% generation transition ($850M)—450 MW solar-storage Q2 like Vista Solar Hub Arizona (300 MW DC/100 MWh Fluence), $300M at 8.5% AFUDC; Oklahoma wind repower $200M, renewables 35% mix vs. 28% two years ago.

25% distribution/resilience ($700M)—$400M Indiana-approved undergrounding/reconductoring 5,000 miles ACCR, $250M add.

AFUDC $180M Q2 at 7.8%.

Headwinds: 20% capex CWIP lag; Ohio $450M case for $1.2B recognition at 10.3% ROE; 8-10% EPC inflation on transformers, mitigated by Siemens/GE deals; NEPA permitting slips $100M; debt 5.2% vs. 9.75% ROE.

Unlocking velocity with formula rates like Entergy, IRPs for EV 25% CAGR, JDA Form Energy iron-air for 50% emissions cut by 2032.

This supports 6-8% EPS CAGR.

On effective cost management, reflected in our dividend policy and payout ratio strategy. Our dividend is key to shareholder value, backed by $28 billion rate base and predictable cash flows from PPAs/wholesale.

27 years consecutive growth at 4.2% CAGR since 1997, like NextEra/Duke. Policy: sustainable growth from internal cash, 65-75% payout of adjusted net income (GAAP EPS ex one-offs).

Q2 quarterly $0.5625/share, 3% up YoY, annualized $2.25—108th increase. FY24 ~$1.1B payout on $3.10-$3.30 EPS guidance. TTM payout 70.2%, below 73% sector median.

Trends: Adjusted EPS $2.95 '22, $3.12 '23, TTM $3.21, 2024E $3.10-3.30; DPS ann. $2.10, $2.18, $2.25, $2.25; payout 68%, 70%, 70.2%, 68-73%; FFO/debt 18%, 19.2%, 19.8%, 20-21%.

Uptrend from higher ROEs—Illinois 9.75%/52.5% equity, ERCOT scarcity.

OCF up 8% to $1.4B Q2, 95% fixed revenues. Yield 4.1% vs. Treasuries 4.3%. Reinvest for electrification: PJM data centers 15% YoY, EV/AI 10-12% to 2030.

Underpinning: 45% capex ($1.9B five-year) 2.5 GW solar-storage like 400 MW Desert Sun ERCOT, >12% IRR post-IRA; $800M AMI/DERMS for 1.2M rooftop solar; nuclear uprate Clinton +$45M, NuScale SMR.

Regional: Midwest 70% payout for transmission; ERCOT 65% for battery arb $120/MWh spikes; SPP 72%.

Reaffirm 68-73% 2024, 4-5% DPS growth 2025. Coverage 1.75x FFO, A- rating.

Engineered for transformation.

The successful integration of our Desert Bloom solar farm has been seamless, contributing immediately to capacity and earnings with its strong performance.

Advancing our Net-Zero by 2045 program ties all this together, with IRA monetization, partnerships, and capex driving value.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Mike Harlan to discuss the financials.

Mike Harlan: Thank you, Lisa. Good morning, everyone. For the Q2, we reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.92—beating our guidance midpoint by 5 cents—and revenue of $2.9 billion, up 4% year-over-year on stronger-than-expected commercial load growth. Our financial performance reflects the strength of our diversified business model and our disciplined approach to capital allocation.

Our capital expenditure for the quarter was $1.1 billion, primarily focused on renewables and grid hardening. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning value to shareholders. We anticipate adjusted diluted EPS for full-year 2024 in the narrowed and raised range of $3.75 to $3.95.

Thank you again, Lisa, and good morning. As we wrap up a solid Q2, our outlook for Q3 and full-year 2024 reflects constructive demand from AI/data centers, execution on our $4.2 billion capital plan, and favorable weather-normalized patterns, offset by higher Northeast natural gas prices and transmission supply chain issues.

For Q3 2024, adjusted diluted EPS of $0.88 to $0.98, midpoint $0.93—3% growth vs. Q3 2023's $0.90. Revenue $2.95 to $3.15 billion, up 5-9% YoY: 6% weather-normalized retail sales, 12% commercial in ERCOT/PJM from hyperscalers, 3% industrial from reshoring, flat residential at 750 CDDs vs. 850.

Adjusted EBITDA $1.05 to $1.15 billion, 7% growth midpoint. Regulated utilities (65% earnings) gain $150 million new rate base from 450 MW solar-storage in CA/FL at 10.2% ROE. CCGTs at 82% CF, heat rates 7,200 Btu/kWh post-upgrades at Susquehanna/Palo Verde.

Opex $650 million up 4% on vegetation/pension; fuel $2.40/MMBtu hedged 85% at $2.25. Capex $1.1B: $400M grid hardening (500 miles 345 kV Southeast), $300M 1.2 GW BESS (Mojave Valley first).

ERCOT merchant gas 2.5 GW captures $40/MWh scarcity; CAISO bifacial solar 800 MW + BESS up 20% QoQ AGC revenue.

Full-year 2024: EPS $3.75-$3.95 (up from $3.65-$3.85, 8% over 2023 $3.57). Revenue $11.9-$12.3B, EBITDA $4.45-$4.65B.

From YTD outperformance ($1.82 Q1/Q2 EPS), $2.3B AFUDC capex (40% clean); load growth 5.5% (data centers 25%); renewables 35% of 18 GW (+1.1 GW, solar CF 28%, wind 36%); nuclear +50 MW to 93% CF; coal Q4 retire, 600 MW CCGT CCUS-ready.

Dividend up 6% $1.92/share ~50% payout; $300M H2 buybacks; M&A renewables SPP $500M +50 bps 2025 EPS.

Risks: weather (+1% EPS/200 CDD), FERC 2222 500 MW DER NYISO upside; regulatory disallowance $100M Texas, gas >$3, IRA credit delays ($250M YTD via JPMorgan).

92% IG balance sheet, 3.4x net debt/EBITDA positions us in power renaissance like Vistra/Constellation.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, Mike. Let me provide an update on the operational front. We are seeing improved efficiency in our gas-fired combined-cycle power plants due to the implementation of turbine upgrades and dispatch optimization software. This has resulted in a 10% increase in output. Our outage rates are also down 15%.

Karen Voss: Thank you, Alex. Turning to our long-term strategy, we are actively exploring opportunities in the battery energy storage space. We believe this will be a key driver of future growth. We are also evaluating potential acquisitions in the ERCOT market.

Brian Walsh: Thank you, Karen. From a technology perspective, we are making significant investments in grid modernization and cybersecurity. We recently deployed an AI-driven cybersecurity solution to enhance our defenses against cyber threats.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Mike, Alex, Karen, and Brian. Now, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Our first question comes from Sarah Jenkins with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins, Goldman Sachs: Thanks, and congrats on a solid quarter, team. First, can you walk us through the drivers behind the 12% beat on adjusted EBITDA of $1.2 billion? Specifically, how much was weather-related versus your thermal fleet optimization and the ramp in renewables? And any color on forward weather-normalized demand growth?

Mike Harlan: Sarah, great question, and thanks for the congrats. The $1.2 billion adjusted EBITDA came in at the high end of our guidance range, reflecting a 12% beat as you noted. Breaking it down: about 40% of the outperformance was weather-driven—Q2 saw hotter-than-normal temperatures across our PJM and ERCOT footprints, boosting cooling degree days by 15% YoY and lifting residential and commercial loads by roughly 8%. Our combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGTs) at the Liberty Peak and Wind River plants ran at 68% capacity factors, up from 62% last year, thanks to our dispatch optimization software from GE Vernova, which shaved $15 million in fuel costs through real-time bidding in the day-ahead markets.

The other 60% was structural: renewables contributed $180 million in incremental EBITDA, with our 1.2 GW solar-plus-storage portfolio in California—anchored by the Mojave Dawn project—hitting 92% availability and capturing $45/MWh in capacity payments under our long-term PPAs with SCE and PG&E. Thermal fleet tweaks, including dry cooling retrofits on our coal-to-gas conversions at the Black Mesa site, added another $50 million in O&M savings. Looking forward, weather-normalized retail load growth is tracking 4.5% for FY24, accelerating to 6% in 2025 on the back of hyperscaler data center contracts—we've signed 800 MW of new load commitments with Microsoft and Google in Texas alone, with in-service dates staggered through 2027.

Operator: Our next question comes from Raj Patel with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Raj Patel, Morgan Stanley: Mike, thanks. On renewables, your queue position in PJM jumped to 4.5 GW after the recent interconnection reforms—how does that position Apex Utilities relative to peers like NextEra or Dominion? And what's the CapEx cadence for your 2 GW battery storage pipeline, including any IRA tax credit monetization?

Lisa Chen: Raj, spot on with the PJM queue dynamics—post the June 2023 reforms, we've cluster-studied and fast-tracked 4.5 GW across solar, wind, and hybrid BESS, with 1.8 GW now in the 'firm service' queue for 2026-2028 in-service. That puts us ahead of Dominion's 3.2 GW but behind NextEra's monster 7 GW; our edge is our 70% brownfield development on existing transmission rights-of-way, minimizing upgrade costs to under $200/kW.

On the 2 GW BESS pipeline—our Sentinel 1 and 2 projects in ERCOT (850 MW/3,400 MWh each) and the ERCOT North hybrid—are fully funded at $1.8 billion CapEx, or $900/kW, blending ITC at 30% plus PTC adders for storage under the IRA. We're monetizing via PTC elections through a $500 million tax equity partnership with KeyBanc and US Bancorp, yielding 8.5% unlevered IRR. Deployment cadence: 500 MW online by YE24, scaling to full 2 GW by 2026, with dispatch revenues projected at $120/MWh from ERCOT ancillary services and EPEX spot pricing. This de-risks our 45% renewables mix target by 2030, up from 28% today.

Operator: Our next question comes from Emily Torres with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Torres, JPMorgan: Good morning, team. With FERC Order 2023 shaking up regional transmission orgs, how are you viewing CapEx escalation for your $5.2 billion five-year plan? Any updates on the SMR pilot at your Hanford site, and thoughts on nuclear credits in the next Farm Bill?

Mike Harlan: Emily, FERC 2023 is a tailwind—it's mandating cost allocation for high-voltage lines, and we've got $1.1 billion in transmission CapEx queued in WECC and SPP for 2025-2027, focused on 345 kV reconductoring to unlock 3 GW of queued renewables. Overall five-year CapEx is holding at $5.2 billion, with 55% growth-oriented ($850 million renewables/BESS, $650 million grid hardening post-Ida and Winter Storm Uri lessons), and AFUDC yielding 7% ROE uplift. Escalation is capped at 4% annually via our EPC fixed-price contracts with Bechtel and Quanta.

On nuclear: our 300 MW SMR pilot at Hanford—partnered with NuScale—is tracking to NRC COL application in Q4 2024, with first pour in 2028. DOE's $1.4 billion matching grant covers 40% of the $2.2 billion build, and we're stacking the zero-emission nuclear PTC at $45/MWh. Farm Bill extension looks likely with bipartisan support—expecting 100% creditability through 2032, positioning us to extend our 1.1 GW fleet life amid data center baseload demand. Peers like Constellation are leading, but our West Coast siting gives us a hydro-nuclear hybrid advantage.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Kim with BofA Securities. Please go ahead.

David Kim, BofA Securities: Thanks, folks. Dividend sustainability looks rock-solid at 65% payout on $2.10 FY24 EPS guidance, but with net debt at 3.6x EBITDA, how are you funding the $1.2 billion M&A war chest for merchant gas and storage bolt-ons? Any color on Texas competition from Calpine or NRG, and ROE impacts from the recent SPP rate case?

Lisa Chen: David, our dividend is a cornerstone—$1.36/share yields 4.2% at current levels, backed by 90% regulated cash flows and a 2.5x interest coverage. Debt metrics are pristine at 3.6x net debt/EBITDA, with $2.8 billion liquidity post our $500 million green bond tap at 4.75% last month.

M&A war chest: $800 million equity from ATM plus $400 million revolver draw, targeting 500-800 MW merchant assets like the Panda Temple gas plant in ERCOT—ROIC north of 12% accretive. Texas is frothy with Calpine's 25 GW fleet and NRG's retail muscle, but our 2.4 GW ERCOT portfolio grew 15% market share via scarcity pricing spikes to $5,000/MWh in July heat domes. SPP rate case settled favorably—9.5% ROE authorized on $3.2 billion rate base, adding $120 million annual revenue, with formula rates kicking in Q1 2025.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the call back over to Lisa Chen for closing remarks.

Lisa Chen: Thank you. In summary, we delivered solid results in the Q2, demonstrating the strength of our business model and our commitment to creating long-term value for our shareholders. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and positioning Apex Utilities for continued success. Thank you for your time and interest in Apex Utilities.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
